client: I've been really struggling since I started this new job at the tech startup about two months ago. It feels like no matter how hard I work or how many hours I put in, I'm always behind on something — there's always another deadline I'm missing or a project that's slipping. Honestly, I'm not even sure talking about it is going to help, because the problem isn't in my head, it's just... there's too much work and not enough time.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a really heavy load right now — constantly feeling behind, no matter how much effort you put in, is genuinely exhausting and demoralizing. I hear your skepticism about whether talking will help, and that's a completely fair thing to wonder. I'm curious though — when you imagine what "enough" would actually look like at this job, does a clear picture come to mind, or does that finish line feel a bit hard to define?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Honestly, when I try to picture what "enough" looks like... it's kind of blurry. Like, I think I'd know it if I got there, but every time I feel like I'm close, someone moves the goalposts — or maybe I move them myself, I'm not sure. That uncertainty is actually kind of unsettling to admit out loud.
therapist: That moment of honesty — recognizing that *you* might sometimes be the one moving the goalposts — takes real courage to say out loud, and it sounds like it landed with some weight for you. This is actually a really important pattern that CBT explores: sometimes our internal standards shift in ways that keep satisfaction just out of reach, no matter what we achieve. I'm wondering, when you do move those goalposts on yourself, what do you think is driving that — is there a fear underneath it, like something bad might happen if you let yourself feel "done"?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Yeah, I think there is a fear underneath it, honestly. Like if I let myself feel done or satisfied, maybe I'll get complacent and everything will fall apart — my work, how people see me, all of it. It's almost like the anxiety is doing a job, keeping me vigilant, and I don't fully trust what would happen if I let it go.
therapist: What you just described is such a clear window into how anxiety can masquerade as a helpful protector — it feels like it's keeping you safe, so letting it go feels genuinely risky, not just uncomfortable. In CBT, we'd call this a "functional belief" about worry itself: the idea that *if I stop being anxious, I'll stop being careful*, which is worth gently questioning together. I'm curious — can you think of any times in your life when you felt settled or satisfied, even briefly, and things *didn't* fall apart?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I mean... yeah, I can think of a few moments, but my brain immediately jumps to "well, those were just lucky." Like, there was a stretch last summer when work felt okay and I wasn't constantly checking my email at midnight, and nothing catastrophic happened — but I keep telling myself that was just a coincidence, not proof of anything. It's hard to trust that, because what if the one time I actually relax is the time something does go wrong?
therapist: That pattern has a name in CBT — it's called "discounting the positive," where your mind accepts the bad as evidence but dismisses the good as luck, which means the scales are permanently tilted against you. What strikes me is that last summer actually *is* real evidence, not a coincidence — your brain just has a rule that says it doesn't count. I'm wondering, what would you need to see, or how many "last summers" would it take, before your mind let that count as actual proof?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I mean, that's an interesting way to put it, "discounting the positive," and I can kind of see what you mean. But honestly, even hearing you say last summer was real evidence, part of me immediately wants to say "yeah but that was one time, and the circumstances were different." I don't know how many times it would take because I feel like my brain would just keep moving the goalposts.
therapist: You're essentially describing the trap in real time — your brain is showing you exactly how it keeps itself safe from ever having to update its beliefs, and there's something almost exhausting about watching it do that, isn't there? What you just said, "my brain would just keep moving the goalposts," sounds less like a defense and more like a tired observation — like part of you is worn out by your own mind's rules. I'm curious, when you notice that exhaustion, does it ever make you want to challenge those rules, or does it mostly just feel defeating?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Yeah, exhausted is exactly the right word. It's like I've been running this mental marathon for years and I can see the finish line but my brain keeps telling me the race is actually longer than I thought. And honestly, it mostly just feels defeating — like, why bother trying to challenge the rules if my mind is just going to rewrite them the second I get close to winning?
therapist: The way you said that — "why bother" — I want to sit with that for a moment, because beneath the exhaustion there's something that sounds less like defeat and more like a quiet kind of grief, like you're mourning the energy you've spent on a race that keeps getting longer. That image you used, the marathon with a moving finish line, is so vivid and real, and I don't think someone who had truly given up would describe it with that much feeling. I'm wondering — underneath the "why bother," is there still a part of you that *wants* to find a way out of this, even if it feels very small right now?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I hate that you're right about that. There is something that still wants to find a way through, but it feels so small and fragile that I'm almost afraid to acknowledge it, like if I say it out loud it'll disappear or I'll jinx it somehow. And then I'll just feel even more foolish for having hoped.
therapist: The fact that you're speaking about that small hopeful part so carefully, almost like you're trying not to startle it, tells me you're already protecting it — which means it matters to you more than "foolish" gives it credit for. Hope that survives years of a moving finish line and this much exhaustion isn't fragile, even if it feels that way right now. What if we treated that small part not as something that could jinx you, but as the most honest thing you've said today?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I want to believe what you're saying, but it almost feels dangerous to let myself do that. Like if I actually treat that hope as something real and honest instead of just... a weird glitch in my thinking, then I'm setting myself up to feel even more crushed if things don't work out. I've been disappointed so many times with this that I've kind of trained myself to keep that part small on purpose, just to survive it.
therapist: What you just described — deliberately keeping hope small as a survival strategy — isn't a flaw or a glitch, it's actually something you learned to do because it *worked*, it protected you when you needed protecting. But I notice there's something tender in the way you're talking about this, like you're not just explaining a coping strategy, you're also mourning the cost of it. I'm wondering — when you imagine a version of yourself that didn't have to keep hope so carefully rationed, what does that person's life feel like?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: That question kind of stopped me for a second, because I don't actually let myself go there very often. When I try to picture that version of me, it feels almost reckless, like I'm standing at the edge of something and one wrong step and I fall. I guess that person's life feels lighter, but also terrifyingly exposed, like there's nothing to catch you when it doesn't work out.
therapist: That image of standing at the edge, feeling lighter but terrifyingly exposed — that's not recklessness, that's what vulnerability actually feels like, and it makes complete sense that it would feel dangerous when you've spent so long building walls to survive disappointment. What strikes me is that "lighter" snuck into your answer, even wrapped in all that fear — your own words are telling you something about what you're longing for. I'm curious, when you imagine that exposed feeling, is there any part of you that also imagines something — or someone — that *could* catch you, even if you don't fully trust it yet?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I sit with that question for a moment, because honestly my first instinct is to say no, there's nobody. But then I think of my friend Dara, who's checked in on me a few times when I've gone quiet, and I feel this weird mix of warmth and guilt about it, like I don't deserve that kind of attention. The scary part is that even imagining leaning on her makes me want to pull back immediately, like I'd rather stay lonely than risk finding out she'd eventually get tired of me too.
therapist: Dara checking in on you when you go quiet — that's not random, that's someone who is paying attention to *you* specifically, and the fact that your first instinct was "nobody" before she surfaced tells me you might be carrying this more alone than you actually have to. That mix of warmth and guilt is so worth noticing, because the guilt part — "I don't deserve that attention" — sounds like it might be one of the deepest rules running underneath everything we've talked about today. I'm wondering, where do you think that belief that you don't deserve to be caught came from?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech
